scores.accuracy_concern: Confirm from the Covinsky 2003 full text that 23%, 12% and 20% are percentages of all 2,293 patients (not of the 35% who declined); the data come from US hospitals in the 1990s, so the era should be stated.
scores.sharpen: Lead with the roughly 23 in 100 who lost function before admission and never regained it on the ward, name the cohort's era, and give the one discharge-letter line (two weeks before: X; now: Y).

scores.accuracy_concern: The studies were in initially high-functioning women aged 70 to 79 in Baltimore (Fried 2001 is cross-sectional); the claim that earlier detection gives strength and balance work 'more to work with' is an inference these sources do not test. Weiss is dated 2011 in the claim and 2012 in the lead.
scores.sharpen: State the population limit plainly and drop the 'more to work with' inference unless an intervention study supports it, keeping the single history question as the payoff.

scores.accuracy_concern: The national survey figure on unpaid help is unsourced, and 'the question that predicts a crisis' is a predictive claim with no evidence behind it; CFS 5 and 6 wording must be checked against the version 2.0 text.
scores.sharpen: Cut the survey claim and the 'predicts a crisis' wording, and shrink the table to four tasks plus the 'who covers?' row so it reads at phone size; differentiate it from C05-09.

scores.accuracy_concern: The 4.0% to 59.1% spread in Collard 2012 reflects different populations as well as different definitions, so it should not be attributed to definition alone; verify the kappa range 0.10 to 0.83 in Aguayo 2017.
scores.sharpen: Lead with the ELSA finding that the same people were classed differently by different scores, and give the prevalence range only once across C05-04 and C05-14.

scores.values_concern: Arguing for need-based rather than age-based frailty identification in general practice is a service-policy position; keep it clearly marked as judgement and avoid implying a view on the GP contract.
scores.accuracy_concern: UK Biobank used a modified frailty phenotype in healthy volunteers, and 'frailty' at 37 to 45 largely reflects chronic illness; the opening has an unfilled number (3 in 100), the 65-and-over contract age limit is unverified, and the Barnett 10 to 15 year wording is 'unsure'.
scores.sharpen: Pick one message (frailty by this definition appears in middle age and is linked with deprivation), give 3 in 100 frail and 38 in 100 pre-frail with the healthy-volunteer caveat, and drop the CFS and Barnett side claims.

scores.accuracy_concern: One 2003 secondary analysis of one trial; goal attainment scaling is unblinded and depends on how goals are set, so its greater responsiveness may partly reflect bias, and 'the measure that found the benefit' assumes the benefit was real.
scores.sharpen: Reframe from 'found the benefit' to 'the only measure that changed', state the bias risk beside the finding, and present goal attainment scaling as an addition to standard scales.

scores.accuracy_concern: Improvement (about 14 in 100) must sit beside worsening (about 29 in 100), which was twice as common; most improvement among frail people was to pre-frail, not to no criteria; Travers 2019 ranked strength training with protein supplementation 'most effective and easiest to implement' from few trials, which is not the same as 'most consistent evidence' or 'enough protein'.
scores.sharpen: Put the worsening figure next to the improvement figure in the first two lines and describe the Travers finding exactly (strength training plus protein supplementation, limited trials).

scores.accuracy_concern: RR 1.06 is a small absolute gain that must be given per 100 from the summary-of-findings table; the community reduction in unplanned admission is low certainty and should be stated as 'may'.
scores.sharpen: Add absolute effects per 100 for hospital and community, trim the card to three rows, and keep C05-20 free of evidence claims so the two do not repeat each other.

scores.accuracy_concern: The Barthel ceiling-effect source is unsure; do not imply that assessment in the home setting improves outcomes, since trial evidence for pre-discharge home visits is limited.
scores.sharpen: Use one concrete example (a person scoring full marks who cannot manage their tablets or shopping) and make clear how it differs from C05-03 if both run.

scores.values_concern: Must not suggest clinicians avoid telling people about risk; the post should keep honesty about vulnerability alongside care with the word.
scores.accuracy_concern: Schoenborn 2018 is one US study of 29 people in focus groups; Warmoth 2016 and the Age UK/BGS report are unverified; 'frail people were more receptive' is from that single small study.
scores.sharpen: Move it to Teaching round or Ask this, since it concerns wording rather than a treatment decision, and name the study size in the post.

scores.values_concern: Must not push people toward burdensome surgery; keep the option that another treatment may be better.
scores.accuracy_concern: The CPOC/BGS guideline full text cannot be opened here and the named optimisable factors are unverified; optimisation or prehabilitation evidence is mixed and largely irrelevant to emergency surgery, so the post should not imply frailty risk is usually modifiable.
scores.sharpen: Verify the guideline's named factors, limit the modifiable-risk point to planned surgery, and vary the opening so it does not echo E134 ('too frail for rehab').

scores.accuracy_concern: Theou 2021 is a single-centre study of 115 patients on a geriatric ward; check who completed the tree, since the study compared tree scores with geriatricians' scores and may not show that the tree improves scoring by untrained staff; the 88.5% figure is agreement between the tree and junior doctors, not junior doctors' accuracy.
scores.sharpen: Frame the tree as a structured aid with reported agreement, not as proof that non-specialists score accurately with it, and make 'record how the score was reached' the main instruction.

scores.accuracy_concern: Qualitative study of 22 people; the claim that routine acute measures do not record these outcomes needs a source or should be framed as a description of common metrics (time in department, admission, length of stay); the severe-frailty finding is cut off in the abstract.
scores.sharpen: Use the participants' own themes on the visual and make the closing a question staff can ask in the first conversation.

scores.accuracy_concern: The 85-and-over figure (about 1 in 4) must come from the Collard full-text age table; the figures are for people living at home and are definition-dependent, and broader frailty-index definitions give higher prevalence at 85 and over.
scores.sharpen: Put 'living at home' in the headline, verify the age-band figures, and name the definitions in one short line on the visual.

scores.accuracy_concern: The CHS overlap percentages must come from the Fried 2001 full text; CHS excluded people with some conditions from the frailty analysis, so the 'lifelong disability' opening is conceptual and not a CHS finding.
scores.sharpen: Build the Venn only from verified CHS figures and label the lifelong-disability line as a conceptual point, consistent with C05-17.

scores.accuracy_concern: Quote the CFS version 2.0 wording exactly on dementia (degree of frailty corresponds to degree of dementia) and on CFS 6 (minimal help with dressing); check licence terms before reproducing scale text.
scores.sharpen: Close with a one-line model referral entry, for example 'CFS 6 (moderate dementia; walks independently)', so the habit is concrete.

scores.values_concern: Touches the 2020 critical care rationing controversy; state the NICE amendment as fact and mark 'should not lower access to treatment' as ethical judgement without implying a position on rationing policy.
scores.accuracy_concern: The NICE NG159 amendment dates and wording need a published source because the NICE page cannot be opened here; 'dependence caused by a stable lifelong disability is not frailty' overstates, since people with lifelong disabilities can also become frail (as C05-25 shows).
scores.sharpen: Source the NICE change from a published report and rephrase to 'should not be scored as frailty on the CFS', so it agrees with C05-25.

scores.accuracy_concern: Check whether eFI2 has replaced the original eFI in UK GP systems by September 2026, or the critique may describe an outdated version; 'people who seldom see the GP score low' is a consequence of design, not a measured finding.
scores.sharpen: State which version is in use now and present under-coding as a design consequence, closing on 'assess the person'.

scores.accuracy_concern: The 30% figure (RR 0.70) is relative and needs the absolute ADL difficulty scores from the full text; the instrumental-activity result was not statistically clear; CAPABLE is not routinely available in the UK.
scores.sharpen: Give absolute scores and make the UK action specific (ask the GP or council for an occupational therapy assessment of the person and the home) without implying the programme itself is on offer.

scores.accuracy_concern: 'A named person responsible for follow-up' is a judgement, not part of the Cochrane definition, and should be marked as a reasonable request; the BGS toolkit and Parker 2018 are unverified.
scores.sharpen: Leave the evidence to C05-08 and make this a pure preparation and follow-up checklist written directly to older people and families.

scores.values_concern: Criticise the labels, not the doctors who write them; avoid implying a profession is careless.
scores.accuracy_concern: Kee and Rippingale 2009 has no abstract and must be read in full before claiming most labelled patients had acute illness; Oliver 2008 was not found; the Curran survey findings are unverified.
scores.sharpen: Read Kee 2009 in full, keep the replacement note on the visual as the payoff, and make the argument distinct from E133 and E153 by focusing on the specific words.

scores.accuracy_concern: Keep odds ratios out of 'times more likely'; confirm the frailty definition behind 20.2% (CFS 5 or more) and the denominator for 37.4% (survivors to discharge).
scores.sharpen: Lead with the roughly 37 in 100 who needed more care after discharge, and choose either this or C05-11 (or pair them explicitly) since they rest on the same study.

scores.values_concern: The comic must not make the mother or son look foolish, and should not imply the older person's own account is less credible.
scores.accuracy_concern: Magaziner 1997 studied people after hip fracture in Baltimore, so it does not show a general pattern for all older people and relatives; one observed attempt is also imperfect evidence of everyday ability; Elam 1991 is unverified.
scores.sharpen: Say the evidence comes from people recovering from hip fracture and present observation as settling the question for that task, not as the final word.

scores.values_concern: A family reading 'CFS 7' or '8' in a letter may be distressed; explain what the score is used for without implying it measures the person's worth.
scores.accuracy_concern: Level 4 ('living with very mild frailty') describes symptoms limiting activities without needing daily help, so 'levels 4 to 8 describe increasing need for help' is wrong at level 4; confirm the two-week and level 9 wording in the version 2.0 text.
scores.sharpen: Correct the level 4 description and add one line on what the score is and is not used for, so the three questions have context.

scores.values_concern: Avoid framing adults with learning disabilities as inevitably frail; keep the focus on earlier review and correct attribution of decline.
scores.accuracy_concern: The 6.6% vs more than 43% 'least frail group' figure is an awkward metric for the public; Evenhuis 2012 prevalence is unverified; the Dutch cohort was drawn from learning-disability services; 'treatable decline attributed to the lifelong disability' is a judgement the studies did not test.
scores.sharpen: Replace the least-frail icon arrays with a verified plain prevalence comparison (for example 50 to 64-year-olds with learning disabilities against much older people in the general population) and say who was studied.

allocation_reason: All 25 score 36 or more with no disqualifying flag, and after collapsing overlapping pairs and clusters (C05-04/14, C05-08/20, C05-11/22, C05-03/09, the CFS cluster and the younger-adult cluster C05-05/17/25) at least 16 distinct strong ideas remain, so the category supports the maximum of 14.
balance_note: The top 14 by score split 8 practitioners (02, 01, 16, 08, 04, 15, 18, 09), 3 public (07, 24, 19) and 3 both (14, 13, 10), so they lean towards practitioners. No 'Who gets left out' post is in the top 14, although the category note is about frailty as a label that shapes decisions unfairly. Consider swapping C05-09 (overlaps C05-03) for C05-17, adding C05-23 or C05-20 for families, and writing C05-14 and C05-10 directly to older readers. Limit the CFS cluster to about three posts (16, 24, plus 17 or 12), and make sure C05-17 and C05-25 agree: frailty can come earlier, but the CFS is not the right tool for it.
